segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll written on the inside and on the back, sealed up with seven seals.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I was weeping bitterly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the elders said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not weep. Look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though slaughtered, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a lyre and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they sang a new song, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you purchased for God those from every tribe and language and people and nation,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you made them a kingdom and priests for our God, and they reign on the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I looked, and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slaughtered to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and dominion forever and ever!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the four living creatures kept saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Amen!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the elders fell down and worshiped.

notes.phrase: a scroll written on the inside and on the back
notes.note: The word means a written document, which in this period was normally a papyrus roll; the King James Version's “book” suggests a bound volume, and nearly all modern translations have “scroll.” Scrolls were usually written on the inner side only, so one written on both sides is unusually full, and the image echoes the scroll shown to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Some punctuate differently: “written inside, and sealed on the back with seven seals.”

notes.phrase: the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
notes.note: Both titles come from Scripture read as promises of a royal deliverer: Judah is called a lion in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9–10), and Isaiah speaks of a shoot and a root from the line of Jesse, David's father (Isaiah 11:1, 10). A first-century Jewish hearer would recognize these as titles of the Messiah descended from David.

notes.traditional: has prevailed / has overcome / has triumphed
notes.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or contest. “Conquer” keeps the note of victory and ties this verse to the promises “to the one who conquers” in the letters to the seven churches; “overcome” can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not disputed, and several modern translations also use “conquer” in Revelation.

notes.phrase: in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders
notes.note: The Greek repeats “in the midst of,” and the exact position is unclear. It may place the Lamb at the center of the throne, surrounded by the living creatures and the elders. It may instead reflect a Hebrew idiom meaning “between,” so that the Lamb stands between the throne with its living creatures on one side and the elders on the other. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

The verb is the usual word for butchering an animal, especially in sacrifice, and for violent killing. “Slain” is traditional but has become a literary word that softens the picture; “slaughtered” keeps the image of a sacrificial animal, with echoes of the Passover lamb and of Isaiah 53:7. Some modern translations already use it.

In the Scriptures a horn is a standard image of strength and royal power, and seven is the number of completeness, so seven horns signify full power. The seven eyes recall Zechariah 4:10, where seven eyes of the Lord range over the whole earth. Whether “the seven spirits of God” means seven angelic spirits or is a symbolic way of speaking of God's Spirit in its fullness is disputed.

The kithara was a hand-held stringed instrument of the lyre family, the standard instrument for accompanying song in the Greek world and, in the Greek Old Testament, in the temple. Most English versions say “harp,” which now suggests a large triangular instrument; “lyre” is closer to what a first-century reader would picture. Standard lexicons give both glosses.

The word refers to all members of God's people as those set apart for him, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

notes.phrase: you purchased for God those from every tribe
notes.note: The Greek text translated here has no stated object for “purchased,” so “those” is supplied. Many later manuscripts add “us,” which the King James Version follows. Most editors consider the shorter reading, found in Codex Alexandrinus, to be original, since “us” fits poorly with “them” in the next verse.

This is the same Greek word that is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament when it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here, in a list covering all humanity, it has its general sense of a people or nation.

The manuscripts are divided between the present tense, “they reign,” printed in the Greek text translated here, and the future, “they will reign”; the two differ by a single letter. Many editors and most modern translations prefer the future. The King James Version's “we shall reign” and “made us kings and priests” follow later manuscripts that put the song in the first person.

candidates.reason: Varies between “book” and “scroll” across versions and books (Luke 4, Hebrews, Revelation), and it interacts with βίβλος and the “book of life” phrases.
Recurs through Revelation and 1 John 3:12; translators split between “slain,” “slaughtered” and “killed,” and the Lamb passages should match across chapters.
Occurs some thirty times in Revelation as a title for Christ; capitalization and the personal pronoun (“he” rather than “it”) need a single decision.
Recurs in doxologies (1 Peter, Jude, 1 Timothy, Revelation), where versions vary between “dominion,” “might” and “power,” and it must stay distinct from δύναμις and ἰσχύς.
Recurs in Revelation 14:2 and 15:2 and in 1 Corinthians 14:7; “harp” and “lyre” are both defensible, and the choice should be uniform.
